title: How to check a billion usernames in 1.2 GB
description:
Storing a billion usernames at 16 characters each takes 16 GB. A Bloom filter answers "is this name taken?" with 1.2 GB instead: a row of 9.6 billion switches. Each name is scrambled by 7 hash functions into 7 switch numbers, and those switches are turned on. To test a new name, hash it the same way: if any of its 7 switches is off, the name was never added, guaranteed. If all 7 are on it's probably taken, but other names may have flipped them; with 9.6 switches per name and 7 hashes that false alarm happens about 1 time in 100, and only those names get checked against the real list. Burton Bloom described it in 1970; Chrome once used one to check links against its list of malicious sites, and databases like Cassandra and Bigtable still use them.

Numbers checked in code: the sizing formulas (9.585 bits per name, 7 hashes, 1.0% false alarms) and a simulation with 100,000 names and 200,000 never-added test names (1.01% false alarms, no false 'free'). Source: Wikipedia, Bloom filter.

facts_checked: Bloom filter: k hash functions set k bits; a test with any bit off means definitely not in the set; false positives possible, no false negatives; optimal k = (m/n) ln 2; fewer than 10 bits per element for 1% false positives; conceived by Burton Howard Bloom in 1970; Google Chrome previously used a Bloom filter to identify malicious URLs; Bigtable, Cassandra use them to skip disk lookups (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom_filter)
1 billion names x 16 bytes = 16 GB; 1% sizing: 9.585 bits per name = 1.198 GB; k = 6.64 -> 7; (1 - e^(-7/9.585))^7 = 1.004% (verify.py)
Simulation: 100,000 names in 958,506 bits, 7 hashes: every added name tests positive; 200,000 never-added names: 1.01% false alarms (verify.py)

beats.say: A billion usernames: 16 gigabytes. Or just 1.2.
It's not compression. You don't keep a single name. You keep a row of switches.
Someone signs up. You need to know, instantly: is that name free?
Step 1: line up 9.6 billion switches, all off. That's 1.2 gigabytes.
Step 2: scramble each name with 7 different hashes. Each one gives a switch number. Flip those 7 on.
Step 3: a new name comes in. Scramble it the same way. If even one of its switches is off, nobody has it. Free, guaranteed.
But all 7 on doesn't prove it's taken. Other names may have flipped them.
With 7 hashes and 9.6 switches per name, that false alarm hits 1 name in 100. Only those get checked against the real list.
So 99 in 100 free names never touch the big list. Chrome once checked links for malware this way.
